questions.q: In a security review, which of these is the strongest evidence that "only logged-in users can read tasks" holds?
questions.explain: Reading code and docs tells you what someone intended. A test that sends the forbidden request proves what the running app does, and it keeps proving it after the review, because it fails the moment the protection disappears.
options: The route file has requireUser in it
The documentation lists the route as "authenticated"
A test calls the route without credentials and gets 401, and would fail if the middleware were removed
The login route rejects wrong passwords

questions.q: Why does the authentication check loop over router.list() instead of a hand-written list of paths?
questions.explain: The typical authentication bug is a new route that nobody protected. A test that asks the router for every route covers it on the day it is added. A hand-written list only covers the routes someone remembered.
options: A route added next month is checked automatically, so a forgotten middleware fails the test without anyone updating it
Because hand-written paths cannot contain parameters like :id
Because the router refuses unauthenticated requests by itself

questions.q: The check also asserts that exactly two routes are public. What does that add?
questions.explain: Without it, anyone could mark a route public and the deny-by-default loop would simply skip it. Pinning the list forces the change through a test edit that a reviewer sees.
options: It makes the test run faster
It stops public routes from being rate-limited
Making a route public becomes a visible decision: adding one fails the test until someone updates it in a reviewed change
It checks that the public routes return 200

questions.q: Linus asks for the id of a task that belongs to Ada. Which answer is safest?
questions.explain: Any difference between "exists but not yours" and "does not exist" lets someone discover which ids are real. The same status and the same body reveal nothing.
options: 403 Forbidden with "This task belongs to another user"
404 Not Found, with exactly the body a missing task gets

questions.q: A client sends POST /tasks with {"title":"Pay rent","ownerId":"u-linus"} while logged in as Ada. What should the Task API do?
questions.explain: Who the caller is comes only from what the server verified. Fields in the body that claim an identity are ignored; the NewTask schema keeps only title.
options: Create the task for Linus, because the client asked for it
Create it for Ada: the owner comes from the verified token, and the schema drops ownerId
Create two tasks, one for each user

questions.q: Why does the review insist on issuer and audience in the token configuration?
questions.explain: The signature only proves "someone with this key made it". The aud and iss claims say who it is for and who made it, and the verifier refuses a mismatch, including a token that has none.
options: A token made for another service is refused even if that service signs with the same key

questions.q: verifyAccessToken(pair.refreshToken, config) returns valid: false. Why is that the behaviour you want?
questions.explain: Refresh tokens live days, access tokens minutes. If a refresh token also opened every route, stealing one would give long-lived access to everything. Separate secrets and a type claim keep them apart.
options: Refresh tokens are expired from the start
A long-lived refresh token must not work as an access token; it is signed with its own secret and only accepted where refreshing happens
Because the refresh token is encrypted

questions.q: Which Set-Cookie line fails the cookie check from the lesson?
questions.explain: SameSite=None sends the cookie with requests started by any other site, which is what CSRF needs. The Task API has no cookie that other sites must send, so the check requires Lax or Strict.

questions.q: Why may requests authenticated with Authorization: Bearer … skip the CSRF token check?
questions.explain: CSRF works because browsers attach cookies automatically. An Authorization header is only sent when your own JavaScript adds it, and a page on another origin cannot read your token to add it.
options: Bearer tokens are longer than cookies
A browser never adds that header by itself, so another website cannot make a user's browser send it

questions.q: Linus logs in, copies his own valid CSRF token, and tricks Ada's browser into posting it together with Ada's cookies. Why does the Task API refuse it?
questions.explain: A CSRF token that is not tied to a session can be taken from the attacker's own account and replayed against a victim. Passing the same sessionId to issue and verify closes that gap.
options: Because CSRF tokens can be used only once
Tokens are issued and verified with a sessionId, so a token from another session does not match Ada's
Because SameSite blocks all cross-site requests

questions.q: A preflight from https://evil.example gets no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header. What does that protect against?
questions.explain: CORS is enforced by browsers, for scripts running on other origins. Direct callers ignore it; authentication, authorization and rate limits stop them.
options: Every script, bot and curl command calling the API
JavaScript on that other site reading the API's responses inside a user's browser

questions.q: The adapter has no trustProxy setting. An attacker sends six login attempts, each with a different X-Forwarded-For. What does the login limiter count?
questions.explain: Without trustProxy the header is just text the client wrote, so the limiter keys on the address of the actual connection. Behind your own proxy you set trustProxy to that proxy, so only its header is believed.
options: Six different clients, one attempt each
Six attempts from one client, the connection's real address, so the sixth gets 429
Nothing: requests with the header are skipped
It refuses every request that has the header

questions.q: https://internal.example.org/hook passes isSafeUrl. Why does the webhook route still resolve the host name?
questions.explain: isSafeUrl can only judge the text of the URL. Where a name points is decided by DNS, so the route checks every resolved address with isPrivateHostname, and the sender checks again at delivery time.
options: To make the request faster later
A public-looking name can point to a private address such as 10.0.0.8, which only a DNS lookup reveals
Because isSafeUrl does not check the scheme

questions.q: A task title is <img src=x onerror="alert(1)">. Which is the right defence?
questions.explain: The text is harmless as data. XSS happens when output is interpreted as HTML, so encode at the place it lands, for that language. Filtering input breaks legitimate text and misses encodings.
options: Store it as typed; return it as JSON with nosniff and a CSP, and escape it wherever it is put into HTML

questions.q: The SQL check ends with check("the scan does spot one", stringBuilt.test("db.query(`…${id}`)")). Why?
questions.explain: A "no problems found" result is only meaningful from a check that can find problems. Testing the scanner on a known bad line shows it actually works.
options: To run the query against the database
To prove the scanner can fail: a pattern that never matches would pass every check forever

questions.q: Why do the path traversal and request smuggling checks write raw HTTP to a socket instead of using fetch?
questions.explain: A URL like /tasks/../../etc/passwd is cleaned up to /etc/passwd by the URL parser before it is sent, and fetch manages framing headers itself. To test how the server treats what a raw client or a broken proxy might send, you send those bytes yourself.
options: fetch normalises paths and refuses conflicting length headers, so it cannot send the requests these checks need
The server does not accept fetch requests

questions.q: What is a canary in this lesson's log check?
questions.explain: Because the test chose the values, it can search every captured line for them. Unlike key-based redaction, this also catches a secret glued into a message string.
options: A logger that only writes errors
A distinctive value (a test password, token or secret) whose appearance in any log line or response proves a leak
A feature flag for new code

questions.q: Why does the log check also assert that "database unavailable" appears in the captured lines?
questions.explain: Absence checks are easy to satisfy by accident: a broken transport, a wrong level, a mocked logger. One presence check shows the lines searched are the real ones.
options: Because the logger needs at least one line to flush
A logger that writes nothing passes every "no leak" check, so the test must also prove that logging works
To make the test fail on purpose

questions.q: Where must the middleware that turns errors into responses go so that error responses carry the security headers?
questions.explain: Middleware runs like nested calls. The security middleware adds headers to whatever its next() returns. An error that escapes past it, or is only turned into a response outside it, gets no headers.
options: After createSecurityMiddleware(), so the security middleware wraps it and decorates the response it returns

questions.q: An app uses createApplication from @zudojs/core and logs { password } on failed logins. What fixes the leak with the published package?
questions.explain: The core ConsoleLogger writes context as given unless a redaction hook is configured. createLogRedactor() is that hook. It is a safety net; the real fix is to never put a password in a log call.
options: Nothing: the core logger redacts passwords by default
Pass logger: { redact: createLogRedactor() } to createApplication, and still stop logging passwords

questions.q: A ConflictError carries metadata: { field, ownerEmail }. What does serializePublicError(error, { publicMetadataKeys: ["field"] }) guarantee?
questions.explain: Without the option, exposed errors publish all their metadata, with only secret-looking key names redacted. The allow-list names exactly what may leave, so new keys stay private by default.
options: The message is replaced with a generic one
Only field is copied into the public metadata; ownerEmail stays on the server
No metadata at all is included

questions.q: Which finding deserves the highest severity?
questions.explain: Severity is impact times likelihood. Reading everyone's private data with a changed number is high impact and trivial to do. A missing framing header on a JSON body is low on both.
options: JSON error bodies from the adapter lack X-Frame-Options
The health route says "ok" without authentication
Any logged-in user can read other users' tasks by changing the id in the URL
Access tokens live 15 minutes instead of 10

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A conflict is a 4xx with expose: true, so by default all of its metadata is published. Only secret-looking key names are redacted, and ownerEmail is not one. The allow-list keeps just field.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A plain Error becomes a non-exposed 500, and serializePublicError replaces the message of a non-exposed error with a safe one. The real message stays for the logs.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: An empty allow-list means no metadata key may leave, so the property is left out entirely. The message stays because a validation error is exposed by design.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Redaction works on metadata key names. The password key is hidden, email is not on the default list, and a value glued into the message string is never seen by the redactor. That second line is what a canary search catches.
options:
login failed {"email":"ada@example.com","password":"[REDACTED]"}
login failed with hunter2 {}

login failed {"email":"ada@example.com","password":"hunter2"}
login failed with hunter2 {}

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The object schema refuses a __proto__ key outright, and it drops keys it does not know, such as ownerId. Both properties are what the Task API relies on for items 2 and 14.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: SameSite=None does not count as protection, and the second cookie lacks HttpOnly. The third has no attributes at all. Even a harmless cookie like a theme should follow the rule, so a check can apply it to every cookie without exceptions.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A prefix test accepts any host that merely begins with your name. An exact comparison with a list is the safe form; the CORS middleware's array option works that way.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: $1 is a placeholder inside an ordinary string, not an interpolation. The second line puts a value into the SQL text. The third is a template literal without ${…}, which is fixed text and safe.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The password was glued into a message, so it appears in the second line. The token was redacted by key name, so its canary never shows up. The canary search finds the leak that key-based redaction cannot.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both failure cases take the same branch and build the same response, so the caller cannot tell them apart. The owner still gets 200.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The second argument allows only https:, so the plain http URL is refused. Loopback addresses are refused however they are written, including the hexadecimal form of 127.0.0.1.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Without a hook the core logger redacts nothing, so the reset token is printed. createLogRedactor redacts its default secret-looking keys (a key containing "token" is one) plus the extra patterns you pass, here email.

questions.q: The review's check helper is below. What does this print?
questions.explain: With no rate limit, the sixth attempt is just another 401, so the first check fails. The helper keeps going so you see every result, and remembers the failure in the exit code, which is what CI reads.
options:
FAIL  the sixth login attempt gets 429
PASS  the first five get 401
exit code 1

PASS  the sixth login attempt gets 429
PASS  the first five get 401
exit code 0

FAIL  the sixth login attempt gets 429
exit code 1

FAIL  the sixth login attempt gets 429
PASS  the first five get 401
exit code 0

questions.q: Write unprotected(routes). It receives route objects like router.list() returns (method, path, metadata) and returns the "METHOD path" strings of every route whose metadata.public is not exactly true, in the same order. Those are the routes the deny-by-default check must call.
questions.explain: Compare with === true, not truthiness: a typo like "yes" must not quietly make a route public. Anything that is not clearly public gets checked.

questions.q: Write cookieReport(line) for one Set-Cookie line. Return "name: ok" when it has HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax or SameSite=Strict, and a Max-Age between 1 and 3600; otherwise "name: FAIL". Attribute names are case-insensitive.
questions.explain: A cookie with no Max-Age lives until the browser closes, which can be weeks; Number(undefined) is NaN, and every comparison with NaN is false, so it fails as it should. A day-long session outlives a 15-minute token.
questions.expected:
access_token: ok
_csrf: ok
sid: FAIL
sid: FAIL

questions.q: Write findLeaks(lines, canaries). canaries is an object of name → secret value. Return the sorted names of the canaries that appear in any of the lines. Also return ["logging broken"] if lines is empty, because an empty log proves nothing.
questions.explain: The search is plain substring matching on the final text, which is why it catches values in messages, nested JSON and stack traces alike. The empty-log case turns "no leaks" from a vacuous pass into a failure.

questions.q: Write toResponseBody(error) that uses serializePublicError from @zudojs/errors and only lets the metadata keys field and limit leave the server. Plain Errors must be normalized first with normalizeUnknownError.
questions.explain: One allow-list covers every error type. The plain error becomes a non-exposed 500 whose message is replaced, so "pool exhausted" and the host name stay in the logs.

questions.q: Write readTask(userId, id) for the in-memory store below. Return { status: 200, body: task } for the owner. For a missing task and for someone else's task, return exactly the same { status: 404, body: { error: "Task not found" } }. Ids that are not of the form t followed by digits are also 404.
questions.explain: One shared response object for every failure guarantees the bodies can never drift apart. Validating the id's shape first means odd input never reaches the lookup at all.

questions.q: Write checkSecrets(env, names). It returns a list of problems, one per name: "NAME is missing" or "NAME is shorter than 32 characters", plus "secrets must all be different" when two present secrets are equal. The messages must never contain a value.
questions.explain: Collect every problem before failing, so one restart fixes them all, and name settings, never values: a wrong secret in an error message has leaked into every log that message reaches.
questions.expected:
[ 'JWT_SECRET is shorter than 32 characters', 'API_KEY is missing' ]
[ 'secrets must all be different' ]
[]

questions.q: Create a @zudojs/logger logger named task-api whose transport prints entry.message and JSON.stringify(entry.metadata), and that also redacts the email key. Log "password reset" with { userId: "u-ada", email: "ada@example.com", resetToken: "r-123" }.
questions.explain: redact.keys adds your own names to the built-in list, which already covers token-like keys such as resetToken. Personal data such as email addresses usually needs adding by hand.

questions.q: Write stringBuiltQueries(source). It returns the 1-based line numbers of every line in source that calls .query( or .exec( with a template literal containing ${.
questions.explain: Line 5 puts the search term into the SQL text; it should be title ILIKE $1 with the value `%${term}%` passed as a parameter. Line 7 is a template literal with no interpolation, so it is fixed text. Line numbers make the report actionable in CI.
